[quote=br_bob;61164869]So what you're telling me is essentially 
If I put down a tripwire and tell me people tripping the wire means death and then somebody does that and well gets blown up it would be my fault? Because I personally would say it's there fault for not doing as they're told[/quote]
That is literally the opposite of what has been said. What you are saying (in this tripwire example of yours) is that if someone broke your laws and then you declared war on them that it would be your fault (the laws are the tripwire and you declaring war would be it blowing up). But no one has said that, because 1. if you did declare war in response to your laws being flaunted that'd be in your right, and because 2. you will never declare war on anyone. So the tripwire will only blow up in your face, not the person who stepped on it.

What has been said is that you can't place a tripwire and then when someone steps on it say "nuh uh, I void that so you never stepped on the tripwire" just because you didn't want to blow it up. You CAN blow the tripwire if you wish, you CAN back down and let them trample on your tripwire if you wish. You can NOT control the other person to say that they didn't step on the tripwire just because realistically you'd respond with war and you don't want to, that is bs. You could also realistically be a massive pushover of a nation who's laws get walked all over, and not have to go to war.

How you respond is all in your control, but you have no control over how others treat your tripwire and trying to void them stepping on it is very clearly godmodding.

[b][pre]Mizrahel Sanctions Act[/pre][/b]
[sub]We shall oppose Israel for it has usurped the rights of Arab peoples.
~ Ruhollah Khomeini[/sub]
]
[i]A direct order from the Supreme Leader? Are you sure?

I have a hand-written letter right here. Bakr pulls out a letter from inside his coat and holds it out. Dawud takes the letter from his hand and tears it open, revealing a small paper within. His eyes dart over its contents before he lets it fall away from his hands and onto his table.

God why now? Surely we could have waited for some sort of instigation? Even framed a hostile act on their part? He brushed a hand through his hair.

We will have to do what he wills. It is rare for him to directly push through such legislation but alas. We should prepare for the economic shortcomings this will have for us. No doubt some others in the international community will not take kindly to this either.

Dawud shook his head. He slouched further into his chair as he pondered the order. Bakr sighed as he looked at his President's despair.

Ill finalise the contents of the act and have it passed in the next session of the Assembly.

Dawud did not even care to acknowledge Bakr as he bowed and walked out of the room.



By order of the President, I have called for this session of the Assembly to be convened. Only two members of this assembly are absent today which means we may comfortably move forward with today's session. I request that the member for Al-Khusumah, Bakr Mansuri, take the floor.

Bakr smoothened his clothing, a habit of his, as he got up from his bench and made his way to the table in the middle of the room. The room itself was in the shape of a semi-circle, with all the members of the Assembly sitting at benches and tables that arced through the room. There was a separate row for the bench of the members of the cabinet.

[b]The Mizrahel Sanctions Act[/b]

Thank you.

I have, by order of the Supreme Leader and President, drafted a comprehensive sanctions act targeting Mizrahel. Many of Mizrahels exports, named within this draft, will be completely embargoed by the Islamic Republic of Dabiristan. Other remaining exports will be subject to massive tariffs that will almost entirely make their imports into Dabiristan, unviable. Beyond trade, other financial actions will be implemented against Mizrahel, including but not limited to, the seizure of Mizraheli state assets and restrictions on currency exchange. Diplomatically, Dabiristan will recall any officials within Mizrahel whilst any Mizraheli officials within Dabiristan will be expelled. Mizrahel will also face visa bans, closure of land-crossings, restrictions on Mizraheli nationals working or studying within Dabiristan, and inspection or seizure of Mizraheli vehicles, ships, or aircraft entering national territory.

As Bakr finished his short introduction to the act, murmurs arose amongst the members of the Assembly. Bakr could clearly make out some of the conversations; perhaps the largest concern was the threat to Dabiristans own economy. He spoke again quickly.

For those concerned about our own economy, we are working rapidly towards bills that will help mitigate negative effects on our economy. We expect to have the most important bills ready by the next session.

Although the assembly was clearly opposed to the act, the knowledge that the Supreme leader himself had ordered this was enough to get most of the opposition parties in line. The ruling partys support of the act was already granted regardless. Following a short debate period, the bill was passed as the President declared the act as urgent By law, any proposal that was declared urgent would have to forgo a proper debate period and be voted on within the same session of assembly it was introduced in. 

The Act passed not because it was the will of the government, but because it had been ordered. That alone was sufficient. The Supreme Leader did not attend, did not speak, and did not need to.

Mizrahel would learn of the sanctions within the hour.[/i]
[/spoiler]
